title: Pentagon Weighs Smaller U.S. Military Footprint in Gulf After Iran War
excerpt: The Department of Defense is evaluating options to reduce troop levels and relocate bases farther from Iran once hostilities end.
body:
• Pentagon is weighing options to reduce its roughly 50,000-troop presence in the Gulf once the Iran conflict concludes, according to reports
  • Plans include relocating major bases from within 300 km of Iran's coast to positions more than 500 km away to reduce missile vulnerability
  • Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, Naval Support Activity Bahrain, and Al Dhafra in the UAE are among installations under review
  • The reassessment follows extensive damage to several U.S. bases from Iranian missile and drone strikes during the conflict

The Pentagon is weighing plans to significantly reduce the U.S. military footprint in the Gulf region once the war with Iran concludes, according to The Washington Post. The potential drawdown would mark one of the most significant shifts in American force posture in the Middle East since the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

Currently, roughly 50,000 U.S. troops are deployed across the region, including two aircraft carrier strike groups — the USS Abraham Lincoln and USS George H.W. Bush — operating in the Arabian Sea. More than 20 warships support a naval blockade that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said the U.S. can maintain "indefinitely."

Bases Exposed by Iranian Strikes

The rethink has been driven in large part by the vulnerability exposed during Iranian retaliatory strikes, which caused extensive damage to several U.S. installations. Satellite imagery analyzed by BBC Verify showed the scale of destruction at bases across the region.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=cVse8TkEwoI

"No one in their right mind would ever put the CENTCOM forward headquarters 100 miles away from Iran, yet that's where it is."

— Retired General Frank McKenzie, former CENTCOM commander

U.S. Central Command has reportedly drafted plans to shift personnel and assets from bases within 300 kilometers of Iran's coast to sites more than 500 kilometers away. The changes could affect thousands of troops stationed at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, Naval Support Activity Bahrain — which suffered extensive damage — and Al Dhafra Air Base in the UAE.

Retired General Frank McKenzie, a former CENTCOM commander, described the current basing pattern as a historical "artifact" that "does not match the reality on the ground," telling Middle East Eye that the U.S. needs to look westward, potentially toward basing in Israel.

Where Forces Could Move

Potential relocation sites include Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and a facility near Duqm in Oman, both of which sit well outside Iran's most effective missile range. The Wall Street Journal has also reported that officials are considering reducing the military footprint in Kuwait while potentially rebuilding the heavily damaged Bahrain naval base.

https://x.com/Truthtellerftm/status/2089186451963384187

However, establishing new bases comes with significant diplomatic and financial hurdles. Qatar spent between $1 billion and $2 billion constructing Al Udeid in 1996 and has invested more than $6 billion in maintenance since then. Countries like Egypt and Saudi Arabia may view hosting U.S. bases as a liability that could attract future attacks or be used as leverage.

Retired U.S. Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery noted that the military is already shifting its reliance. "We're not relying on them in the same way that we did before the war," he told Fox News. "I think we are going to reposition these forces."

Impact on Gulf Security Architecture

Any drawdown would have ripple effects across the Gulf, where millions of South Asian workers — including an estimated 8 million Indians — live and work under the security umbrella that American military presence has traditionally provided.

Gulf states have already been diversifying their security relationships in response to the conflict. The broader question, as analysts at the Council on Foreign Relations have framed it, is whether Washington can execute a managed drawdown that preserves regional partnerships, or whether deteriorating conditions will force an involuntary exit.

What's Next

For now, the administration has made clear that any troop reduction is contingent on a final peace deal with Iran. A memorandum of understanding signed in June collapsed within weeks, and negotiations remain stalled. "We want to see that the Iranians do what they promised," a senior U.S. official told reporters.

The Pentagon's internal review is expected to take months, with any concrete basing decisions unlikely before a durable ceasefire is in place. In the meantime, the debate over America's Gulf posture has shifted from whether to draw down to how — a question with profound implications for regional stability and the millions of civilians living across the Gulf.
